criterion_notes.c1: Examines community and household water and sanitation service provision and access (water points, water kiosks, structure-based shared toilets, and public toilets) alongside education, healthcare, and solid waste management in two urban informal settlements in Nairobi, Kenya.
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies both readings of Criterion 2. Under the plain wording, the paper explicitly examines formal and informal governance, institutional rules (via Ostrom's common-pool resource design principles), regulatory ambiguity, and local leadership in service provision. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading, the paper empirically examines concrete rule-type mechanisms directly governing water and sanitation access: (1) boundary and payment-enforcement rules (structure owners physically locking water points and toilet facilities to restrict access to paid residents, and providers withholding services until payment); (2) graduated sanctions and enforcement (denying service access, eviction from structures, and reporting toilet-rule violations or water-point vandalism to local chiefs/police); (3) tariff/cost-recovery rules and regulatory vacuum (absence of pricing guidelines for public toilets causing non-use or user debt, alongside negotiated payment accommodations); (4) informal market-entry regulation requiring existing utility/water vendor approval before new vendors operate; and (5) plot-ownership/tenure barriers and unclear municipal guidelines on operational hours and facility siting.
criterion_notes.c3: Primary qualitative empirical study collecting and analyzing 40 in-depth interviews (36 informal service providers and 4 local leaders) conducted March-May 2022 in Korogocho and Viwandani, analyzed using thematic framework analysis in NVivo 12. Qualitative socio-legal/institutional studies are eligible for the systematic review and mechanism synthesis.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports qualitative access, exclusion, availability, and affordability outcomes for water and sanitation, including physical exclusion via locked water points and toilets for unpaid users, sanctioned denial of service access, non-use of public toilets when needed or user indebtedness due to unregulated fees, long queues at water and sanitation points, and violent payment disputes at water kiosks.
criterion_notes.c5: Population (40 purposively sampled informal service providers and community leaders in Korogocho and Viwandani, Nairobi; unit of analysis is informal service providers and settlement-level governance arrangements affecting resident access), exposure (Ostrom-type informal governance rules and formal policy/regulatory gaps), outcome (resident access, physical exclusion, queues, and fee-related non-use/debt in water and sanitation), and study design (participatory qualitative in-depth interview study with thematic framework analysis) are all clearly identifiable.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is written in English (interviews conducted in English or Swahili and transcribed into English).

evidence_quotes.quote: This study employed qualitative research methodology, utilizing in-depth interviews with 36 informal service providers operating in the education, healthcare, water, sanitation, and solid waste management sectors.

Structure owners would initiate locking water points and toilet facilities for use by specific individuals who had fully paid for the services requirement in their structures, without interference by government officials like public health officers.
As such, without the external actors, water, health, solid waste management (SWM), and sanitation service providers would set boundaries on services to clients until they could pay as agreed.

Those offering sanitation services in public toilets and do not have guidelines on how much it cost to use the facility, leads to many challenges including not using a facility when needed or being forced to get into debts for using the facility.

raw_response.exposure: Informal and formal-interface service governance rules and regulatory gaps: payment-linked boundary/exclusion rules (locking water points and toilets), flexible payment/operational accommodations, informal vendor market-entry approval rules, monitoring and graduated sanctions (service denial, eviction, reporting to chiefs/police), plot-holder land-use barriers, and unclear municipal policies/guidelines on public toilet tariffs and facility operational hours.
raw_response.outcome: Household/resident water and sanitation service access, exclusion, availability, and affordability: restricted/locked access to structure water points and toilets based on payment, sanctioned denial of service access, non-use of public toilets when needed or falling into debt due to unregulated user fees, long queues at water and sanitation points, and payment conflicts at water kiosks.
raw_response.population_and_sample: 40 purposively sampled participants across two urban informal settlements (Korogocho and Viwandani, 20 per site) in Nairobi, Kenya: 36 informal service providers operating ~8 years on average serving residents including vulnerable groups (Table 2 reports 8 water, 8 sanitation, 8 solid waste management, 8 education, and 4 healthcare providers; text on p. 6 has a minor typo stating water n=2 per site) plus 4 community/local leaders. Unit of analysis: informal service providers and settlement-level service governance arrangements affecting resident access.
raw_response.rationale: This primary qualitative empirical study (40 in-depth interviews in two Nairobi informal settlements) examines water and sanitation service provision alongside three other basic services using Ostrom's institutional rule framework. It satisfies both the plain and narrow 2026-10-13 readings of Criterion 2 by analyzing concrete formal and informal rule-type mechanisms governing water and sanitation access—including payment-enforced physical locking of water points and shared toilets, graduated sanctions denying service access, informal vendor entry rules, land/plot tenure barriers to siting public toilets, and the absence of pricing and operational-hour regulations for public toilets and water points—and links them to resident access, exclusion, queues, non-use when needed, and user debt. Per review rules, qualitative socio-legal/institutional studies with identifiable mechanisms and access outcomes are included for narrative/mechanism synthesis.
raw_response.study_design: Participatory qualitative study using in-depth interviews (IDIs) and thematic framework analysis guided by Ostrom's common-pool resource self-governance theory
